The speaker mentioned yesterday that if you open an old book on probability theory, you will see probability introduced as: there is an infinitely repeatable experiment; we do the experiment; we get results; we divide the number of outcomes of interest by the total number of experiments; that ratio tends to the probability.
The old book is a very good book.
That frequency-based definition of probability is completely correct.
When the frequency-based definition is applicable, it is completely correct.
For the coin toss, the frequency-based definition is exactly how we define probability.
In real life and especially in machine learning, we usually want to reason about the probability of events that are not repeatable experiments.
For a bookmaker, they need to predict the probability of Spain winning the FIFA World Cup this year.
There will be only one World Cup this year.
The World Cup is not a repeatable experiment based on previous World Cups.
The teams in previous World Cups were completely different.
Everything in previous World Cups was completely different.
We might want to set probabilities for events that already happened.
Such events are already set, but we just don't know the answer.
In these kinds of cases, it makes no sense to talk about experiments repeated to infinity.
There is a hypothesis that the Odyssey by Homer was not written by the same Homer as the Iliad.
The hypothesis suggests the Odyssey was written by a woman due to lexicographic analysis of the text.
The speaker is not sure about the current status of that hypothesis.
At one time when the speaker checked, it was a hypothesis.
We don't know the answer to the authorship question.
It makes sense to want to assign probabilities to hypotheses like the authorship hypothesis.
There is only one Odyssey.
The Odyssey was written by somebody thousands of years ago.
The answer to who wrote the Odyssey is already set.
We just don't know the answer.
In real life, probabilities are often not limits of ratios of experiments.
In real life, probabilities are degrees of belief.
Probabilities are representations of our uncertainty.
This framing (probabilities as degrees of belief) is very useful for thinking about probability.
This framing is a very useful way to understand what we are doing in machine learning.
When doing machine learning with a real dataset and a real model, we are not getting a logical conclusion.
We are updating our beliefs.
If we have a good, large enough dataset, our beliefs can become much more certain.
With a large enough dataset, confidence intervals may shrink.
We can become more sure in the hypothesis we are evaluating.
We will never be completely sure.
In machine learning, it is all about noisy datasets.
We are combining all evidence to understand something about the model (model parameters in this case).
The result is always a probability distribution.
The point that the result is always a probability distribution often gets lost for people.
The speaker wants to give the general notion of what the class is doing today.
The class is using this identity and reasoning by the base rule.
In deep learning practice, what is actually done all the time is composing a loss function.
A typical loss function is log p(d|theta) + log p(theta).
We take a minus of that because the loss function is to be minimized, not maximized.
In practice, that is the loss function for a neural network.
The class will see how it works specifically today.
Then you minimize the loss function with respect to theta (the neural network parameters).
You get theta MAP (maximum a posteriori estimate) by minimizing.
Theta MAP is the argmin of the loss function.
Theta MAP is the maximum posterior hypothesis.
Theta MAP is the argmax of p(theta|d).
Very often, people stop at theta MAP when thinking about deep learning and neural networks.
The process often stops here.
Then people say they now know theta.
They say they got their model checkpoint.
They say they have the true weights.
That (stopping at theta MAP and considering it the true weights) is an oversimplification.
In practice, very often we will obtain theta MAP and use theta as a point estimate.
It is very helpful to remember that theta MAP is just a point estimate.
Theta MAP is just the maximum of a whole distribution.
In deep learning with huge neural networks, we usually cannot sample several different points from the posterior distribution.
If we could sample from the posterior distribution, it would be very helpful.
Sampling several different points from the distribution would allow seeing how that translates into different predictions.
Sometimes you see this (sampling from the posterior) in deep learning as well.
All of this machinery is about degrees of belief.
This machinery is about our uncertainty.
Our original uncertainty is captured in P(theta).
That uncertainty is reduced by D (the data we get).
Our new uncertainty is captured in P(theta|D).
We know something about the parameters.
It cannot be that we know absolutely nothing about the parameters.
Sometimes it can be that we know absolutely nothing.
Even when we know nothing, we still need to express it in a distribution.
When we get new information, we update.
After updating, we have some new belief about theta.
The new belief about theta is a distribution.
The belief is uncertain.
The belief is never just a single point.
This is what the speaker wanted to say here.

The speaker suggests trying an example with the students.
Here is a very standard trick question from probability theory.
The question involves a person who has two kids.
The speaker's acquaintance has two kids.
The speaker has never met the kids.
The speaker does not know their names.
The speaker does not know their genders.
Assume every baby is either a boy or a girl with probability 1/2 each.
Assume the gender of the first baby is independent from the gender of the second.
The two kids are just there.
Each kid is like a fair coin to us in terms of being a boy or a girl.
The speaker goes to the person and asks: "Do you have any boys?" i.e., among the two children, are there any boys?
The person says yes.
In this setting, the question is: what is the probability that he has a girl?
The speaker rhetorically asks how many and how one would arrive at the answer.
We know that he has at least one boy.
There is one slot available that can be either a boy or a girl.
That (the one-slot reasoning) is not quite right.
The speaker asks for other ideas.
What is the probability space here? What are the possible outcomes?
An earlier suggested answer is not quite true.
This is a straightforward trick question.
It would usually trap people unless they know it.
The person has two children.
It is like child number one and child number two.
For every child, there are two possibilities (boy or girl).
There are four options in total.
The answer four is exactly right.
There are four possibilities for the genders of two children: boy-boy, boy-girl, girl-boy, and girl-girl.
In the prior, before any information is known, these four possibilities are equally likely.
Each possibility has a probability of one-fourth.
When information "there is at least one boy" is obtained, the possibility girl-girl is eliminated.
The answer "yes" to "do you have any boys?" does not distinguish among the remaining three possibilities.
After eliminating girl-girl, the three remaining options are boy-boy, boy-girl, and girl-boy, and they remain equally probable.
Two of these three options contain a girl.
Therefore, the probability of having a girl given that there is at least one boy is two-thirds.
Formally, the probability can be computed as P(girl | boy) = P(MF or FM) / P(MM, MF, FM), where MF is boy-girl, FM is girl-boy, and MM is boy-boy.
This equals (2/4) divided by (3/4), which simplifies to 2/3.
In a separate scenario where a person meets one of the two children and that child is a boy, the probability that the other child is a girl is one-half.
Meeting a specific child fixes the gender of that child.
For example, if the first child is known to be a boy, the possible outcomes are boy-boy and boy-girl, which are equally likely.
In that case, one of the two outcomes has a girl, so the probability is one-half.
The two-child problem illustrates Bayesian reasoning even without explicitly using Bayes' theorem.
In Bayesian reasoning, one starts with prior beliefs (for example, that all gender combinations are equally likely).
Upon receiving evidence, one updates the beliefs based on that evidence.
There are additional examples that demonstrate potential pitfalls of Bayes' rule.
A murder occurred, and blood left at the crime scene is known with certainty to be the killer's blood.
The blood type is rare: only 1% of the population has it.
The defendant in the murder trial has this blood type.
The prosecutor argues that the chance the defendant would have this blood type if innocent is only 1%, so the defendant is guilty with probability 99%.
The prosecutor's argument is incorrect.
The mistake is equating P(blood type | innocent) with P(guilty | blood type).
In a court of law, the goal is to determine P(guilty | evidence).
The prosecutor's conclusion of 99% is about P(guilty | blood type).
The prosecutor correctly estimates P(blood type | innocent) = 1%.
The prosecutor incorrectly computes P(guilty | blood type) as 1 - P(blood type | innocent) = 99%.
The prosecutor's reasoning equates P(guilty | blood type) with P(blood type | guilty), which is incorrect.
The correct approach uses Bayes' theorem: P(innocent | blood) = [P(blood | innocent) * P(innocent)] / P(blood).
The prior probability of innocence and the overall probability of the blood type can significantly affect the result.
For example, if there are two possible suspects and both have the blood type, the blood type evidence provides no discriminatory power.
In that scenario, the probability of guilt for each suspect remains one-half.
The prosecutor's reasoning would still assign each suspect a 99% probability of guilt, which is absurd.
The defense attorney points out the prosecutor's mistake and offers an alternative calculation.
The defense notes that in a city of one million people, approximately 10,000 would have the rare blood type.
Based solely on the blood type evidence, the probability that the defendant is guilty is about 0.01%.
The defense argues that this evidence is very weak and should not be admitted.
The defense attorney's reasoning is also flawed.
The defense attorney's reasoning assumes that every person with the blood type in the city has an equal chance of being the murderer, ignoring other reasons the defendant is a suspect.
O.J. Simpson was a successful American football player in the 1980s.
Simpson had a history of domestic violence against his wife.
Simpson's wife was killed, and Simpson was tried for murder.
The murder trial was highly publicized in the 1990s.
The prosecution presented evidence of Simpson's history of violence against his wife.
The defense attorney acknowledged that beating one's wife is wrong.
The defense presented a statistic: only one in 2,500 women subjected to domestic violence are killed.
The defense concluded that domestic violence evidence is irrelevant to the murder charge.
The court agreed with the defense's argument and instructed the jury to disregard the domestic violence evidence.
The O.J. Simpson case is another example of the prosecutor's fallacy, where a conditional probability is misinterpreted.
In the O.J. Simpson trial, the appropriate question was P(history of domestic violence | wife was murdered), not P(wife was murdered | history of domestic violence).
The defense's statistic, P(murdered | domestic violence), considers a population where no murder has yet occurred.
In a murder trial, because the murder has already occurred, the relevant probability is not P(murder | domestic violence) but the reverse.
In the vast majority of the 25,000 cases from the defense statistic, no murder occurred.
In the example under discussion, certain factors are not included in the conditional probability calculation.
Using the exact same statistics available at the time, the correct conditional probability is estimated to be approximately 7/8.
Among women who were murdered and had a history of domestic violence, in the vast majority of cases, the husband committed the murder.
If the evidence in this case had been presented correctly, it would have looked completely different.
This situation illustrates that people make mistakes in estimating conditional probabilities.
It is a good habit to understand exactly what one is trying to estimate.
In life, all decision-making involves estimating various conditional probabilities.
It is a good habit to explicitly understand the exact probability being evaluated, even if one cannot compute it exactly.
In real life, we do not have the kind of statistics needed to compute such probabilities exactly, so we cannot run the numbers.
If you qualitatively understand what is on the left and right of the vertical bar in a conditional probability, things become clearer in many cases.

The lecture proceeds to the first real example.
The speaker will present two examples today: linear regression and logistic regression.
Linear regression and logistic regression will not be discussed in great detail, but they are directly relevant to neural networks.
The simplest possible neural network is a linear model, specifically a neural network consisting of one perceptron.
Linear regression and logistic regression are still directly relevant to modern neural networks, and the speaker will explain why.
The speaker hopes that the audience has some intuition about linear regression, even if they do not remember formulas or have never studied it systematically.
Linear regression is point number two in the lecture.
In linear regression, there are input x and target variable y, with data points plotted.
An assumption is made in linear regression that there is a linear dependence between x and y, with noise.
In linear regression, the data points are not exactly on a straight line but are close to a straight line.
The problem of linear regression is to find the straight line that fits the data.
In two-dimensional drawings, x is one-dimensional.
In reality, the target variable y is a scalar number.
In reality, x is typically a vector, and y is modeled as a linear combination of the x's.
The speaker will skip the intercept term in the linear model description.
Without the intercept, y is written as the dot product of weight vector w and input vector x.
The dot product is w1*x1 + ... + wd*xd.
To omit the intercept, an extra constant dimension (x0=1) is added to the input vector.
By extending x with a constant 1, the dot product with w automatically includes the intercept term.
This is a standard trick used to avoid explicitly writing the intercept term w0.
In linear regression, the goal is to minimize a measure of error between actual values and predictions.
The most common error measure is the sum of squared differences (squared error).
The standard linear regression approach finds weights W such that the predictions W*X_n are close to the actual Y_n, as measured by the sum of squared distances (Y_n - W*X_n)^2.
Standard linear regression minimizes this squared loss with respect to the weights W.
Squared loss is used because it is symmetric and penalizes errors in both directions equally.
There are many other symmetric monotone functions of distance that could be used as loss functions, such as absolute error, fourth power, exponential of absolute value.
Minimizing different loss functions would lead to different optimal weights w.
The reason for using the squared loss in linear regression stems from probabilistic assumptions.
Linear regression can be framed as a machine learning model.
In this machine learning framing, the parameters theta correspond to the weights w.
The data consist of inputs X and outputs Y.
The likelihood is P(D|theta), the probability of the data given the parameters.
A standard assumption in machine learning is that data points are conditionally independent given the parameters.
In supervised learning, we model only the output Y given the input X; the input X appears on the right-hand side of the conditional.
The distribution of Y given the model and input x is what needs to be defined in the probabilistic framework.
The second assumption is linearity: the most probable value (center) of this distribution is w times x.
To enable learning, a full probability distribution around w times x must be defined.
This distribution should be symmetric and decrease to both sides.
Larger distances from w times x should be less probable.
To find the maximum likelihood line, we want the distances (errors) to be as small as possible.
The specific loss function depends on the chosen distribution for the errors.
There are many bell-shaped, symmetric distributions to choose from.
The most natural default distribution for the errors is the Gaussian (normal) distribution.
The Gaussian distribution is chosen because of the central limit theorem.
The central limit theorem provides the theoretical justification for using the Gaussian distribution in this context.

The central limit theorem states that if you take a large number of independent samples from any distribution and compute their average (or sum), the distribution of that average (or sum) approaches a Gaussian distribution.
In a physical process where many small independent sources of noise add together, the resulting total noise tends to be Gaussian or close to Gaussian.
In a high school physics experiment of rolling a ball down a slope to measure distance, the ball experiences billions of small impacts as it rolls.
These small impacts come from imperfections in the plane.
These small impacts come from imperfections in the ball.
These small impacts come from wind or other factors.
Each individual imperfection or small impact is not Gaussian.
Each small impact likely acts in a specific direction.
When all these small impacts are added together, the total effect is Gaussian because there are many of them.
There is a mathematical theorem (the central limit theorem) that provides the basis for the convergence to a Gaussian.
When you average many small notches that act in different directions, the result is approximately Gaussian, provided there is no systematic bias.
If all the small notches act in the same direction, the result is not Gaussian.
Because of the central limit theorem, it is most natural to model the error in linear regression with a Gaussian (normal) distribution.
The normal distribution is called "normal" because it naturally arises from the addition of many small effects.
The normal distribution is important because of this property of arising from many small effects.
If you only look at the shape or density of the normal distribution, you would not understand why it is special.
The normal distribution is special because of the central limit theorem, which says that many sums converge to a Gaussian.
In linear regression, we assume that the target variable yn follows a normal distribution centered at w xn with variance sigma^2.
This normal distribution for yn is a one-dimensional Gaussian.
In linear regression, it is assumed that the mean of yn is a linear function of xn: w xn.
In linear regression, it is assumed that the noise (error) is Gaussian.
The probability density function of the Gaussian distribution for yn given parameters w and sigma is 1 / sqrt(2πσ²) * exp( - (yn - w xn)² / (2σ²) ).
To find the maximum likelihood estimate for the weights w in linear regression, one must maximize the likelihood function.
In machine learning, the likelihood function is often a product over many data points.
Multiplying many probabilities (likelihoods) can lead to numerical difficulties.
The standard trick to handle a large product of probabilities is to take the logarithm, converting the product into a sum.
Taking the logarithm is the first step when maximizing the likelihood.
The log-likelihood for linear regression under Gaussian noise is sum over n of [ -1/2 log(2πσ²) - 1/(2σ²) (yn - w xn)² ].
The log-likelihood simplifies to -N/2 log(2πσ²) - 1/(2σ²) sum over n (yn - w xn)², where N is the number of data points.
The term -N/2 log(2πσ²) is constant with respect to w.
The goal in maximum likelihood estimation is to maximize the log-likelihood with respect to w.
Maximizing the log-likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared errors: sum (yn - w xn)².
This provides the motivation for using the sum of squares (rather than absolute values or other loss functions) in linear regression.
There is a fourth assumption in linear regression: the variance of the noise is constant across the entire dataset.
In statistics, this constant variance property is called homoscedasticity.
Homoscedasticity means the noise variance is constant.
The homoscedasticity assumption allows pulling sigma² out of the sum in the log-likelihood, making it irrelevant for maximizing with respect to w if sigma is fixed.
In practice, the homoscedasticity assumption can be violated.
For example, data points may start out dense (low variance) and later become more noisy (higher variance), yet one might still want to fit a single straight line.
If homoscedasticity is violated, the loss function needs to be modified.
Detecting such violation and understanding its implications for the loss function is non-trivial.
One reason to understand the probabilistic approach is to notice when the assumptions behind the sum of squares are violated.
Understanding the assumptions helps in recognizing when the standard method (minimizing sum of squares) stops working.
An example of assumption violation is when the variance changes partway through the process.
Another example is when the noise is believed to be only in one direction (e.g., only positive).
In such cases, one might need an asymmetric noise distribution, such as one supported only on the positive part of the line.
There exist variations of linear regression that handle non-standard noise distributions.
Handling non-standard noise distributions requires noticing the violation and applying the appropriate mathematical framework.
In a Bayesian approach, the goal is not to maximize the likelihood p(D|w) but to compute the posterior p(w|D).
The Bayesian approach requires specifying a prior distribution on the weights w.
For linear regression, the prior is a more complicated construct.
Bayesian inference in linear regression involves continuous distributions, making the probability theory messier compared to simple discrete cases like coins.
In coin flipping, the likelihood was discrete (two outcomes), but the prior and posterior became continuous.
In linear regression, because there are multiple weights, the prior must be a multi-dimensional distribution.
Maximizing the posterior distribution p(w|D) changes the optimization problem only slightly.
The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior, with a constant that does not affect maximization.
Maximizing the posterior is equivalent to maximizing the sum of the log-likelihood and the log prior.
The log prior term in the optimization is commonly referred to as a regularizer.
Regularization corresponds to imposing a prior distribution on the model parameters.
In practice, the regularizer is the part of the loss function that depends only on the model parameters (weights) and not on the data.
Formally, the regularizer represents prior beliefs about the weights before seeing the data.

It may seem strange to have a prior for linear regression weights because, unlike coins (where we have strong prior beliefs that they are fair), we typically have no intuition about which slope is more likely.
Without data, all slopes in linear regression might seem equally plausible.
To illustrate the role of the prior, one can turn a one-dimensional regression into a multi-dimensional one by extracting additional features from X.
In simple applications of linear regression, people sometimes directly use the original input X as a number, modeling the output as w X.
More commonly, before learning the weights, one extracts features from the input X, denoted as φ(X).
Linear regression is then performed on the feature vector φ(X), with output w·φ(X).
Sometimes feature extraction reduces the dimensionality or content; for example, doing linear regression directly on image pixels makes no sense.
When applying linear regression to images, one should first extract semantically rich features and then apply linear regression.
Sometimes the opposite is true: the original input X is very simple, and to capture a more complex relationship between X and Y, one extracts additional features.
The example considers one-dimensional regression.
In one-dimensional regression, there is only one X variable and one Y variable.
The data points do not look linear; they look like a parabola (quadratic function).
Linear regression can fit a quadratic function by transforming x into a feature vector (1, x, x^2).
The loss function minimized is the sum of squared errors: sum over n of (y_n - (w0 + w1*x_n + w2*x_n^2))^2.
The fitted model is a parabola.
Deep learning neural networks learn good feature extractors.
Before deep learning, machine learners manually designed feature extraction and then applied relatively simple models.
In neural networks, feature extraction is part of the model and has learnable weights.
In a neural network for image input, after many layers, a vector of numbers goes into the final layer.
For neural networks predicting a number (regression), the last layer is typically a linear layer.
The layers before the final layer perform feature extraction; the final layer performs linear regression on these extracted features (not on raw input).
Learning the feature extraction layers is the hard part; the final linear regression layer is easier.
Neural networks for regression usually end with linear regression; for classification, they end with logistic regression.
The rest of the network extracts features for the final layer, so linear models remain relevant for deep learning.
The speaker shows a polynomial regression problem.
The true function is a sine wave, which is not a polynomial.
The data points are taken from one period of the sine wave.
In the plot, stars represent data points, horizontal axis is x, vertical axis is y; there is one dimension.
The points are not linear; linear regression yields a straight line with high error.
A polynomial of degree three is a good fit for these points.
A parabola (degree 2) is slightly better than linear but still doesn't capture the pattern well.
A third-degree polynomial can have one minimum and one maximum, matching one period of a sine wave.
Training a third-degree polynomial regression (with four weights including intercept) gives a good fit.
The errors for the third-degree polynomial fit are fine.
Increasing the polynomial degree to 4 or 5 yields curves that look approximately the same as degree 3.
Degree 4 and 5 curves are slightly better but similar.
The model will break (become bad) if the degree is increased too much, maybe at 10 or 20.
With 11 data points, a polynomial of degree 10 can pass through all points exactly (interpolate).
A degree-10 interpolation polynomial has zero training error but large test error and is useless for prediction.
The interpolation polynomial has strange peaks.
The degree-10 model is much worse than the degree-3 model; this is a classic example of overfitting.
Overfitting occurs because the model has too many parameters.
In one-dimensional problems, one can visually choose the polynomial degree; in high dimensions, visualization is impossible.
In high-dimensional linear regression, overfitting can happen when adding polynomial features.
If simple linear regression fails, one might try a quadratic dependency by adding quadratic features.
In one dimension, adding quadratic or higher-degree features adds only one feature at a time, allowing fine control.
For a d-dimensional input, the quadratic feature vector includes 1, all x_i, all squared terms, and all interaction terms x_i*x_j.
The number of quadratic features is on the order of d^2.
For input dimension 100, the number of quadratic features is approximately 5,000.
Increasing features from 100 to 5,000 can cause overfitting.
In high dimensions, there is no gradual way to add polynomial features; the feature count jumps dramatically.
Not all quadratic features are needed; only some interactions matter.
The learning process must determine which interactions matter because they are not known in advance.
In statistics, features like x1*x3 are called interactions.
To discover which interactions matter, one likely needs to include all of them initially.
Overfitting is inherent in machine learning, even for linear regression, and especially for neural networks.
To detect overfitting without visual inspection, a simple principled approach is to use a test set.
A validation set is set aside from the data points.
The error on the validation set is measured.
Training is stopped when the validation set error starts to increase.
This stopping when validation error increases is a standard procedure in machine learning.
If this procedure can be performed, it is acceptable.
In the discussed example, this procedure cannot really be used.
One could imagine adding quadratic terms one by one.
Adding quadratic terms one by one would require going through all terms and then going through them again.
This iterative process would probably be impractical.
Adding all quadratic terms at once leads to overfitting.
When all terms are added at once, there is no continuous process that can be stopped to prevent overfitting.
Another symptom of overfitting is the behavior of the model coefficients.
For polynomial fits, as the polynomial degree increases, the coefficients grow in a bounded way before overfitting.
When overfitting starts, there is a sudden jump in the coefficients.
In the example, overfitting occurs at degree 10, but it could happen a bit earlier.
Overfitting is indicated by coefficients around ±50.
This observation about coefficients is a tricky and not entirely formal part.
In this example, there are 10 or 11 data points.
The x values range from approximately -1.5 to +2.
The y values range from -1 to +1.
A model with coefficients around 50 seems implausible for describing these points.
This implausibility is the intuitive reading of the coefficient jump.
The formal interpretation is that prior belief about the coefficients should be that they are relatively small.
For this dataset, coefficients should be on the order of ±1 or ±2, definitely not ±50.
In standard linear regression with one-dimensional x, the weight space is two-dimensional.
In quadratic regression, the weight space is three-dimensional.

To solve the overfitting problem, one can add a prior distribution that the weights are relatively small.
The prior distribution P(W) should be concentrated around zero.
All weight vectors should have non-zero density, but the density should be highest near zero.

The Gaussian prior is centered at zero with some covariance matrix.
With no prior distinction between weights, the covariance matrix is the identity matrix.
An identity covariance matrix implies the prior assumes weights are independent.
The log of the Gaussian prior is a constant minus (1/(2 σ₀²)) times the sum of squares of the weights.
Adding this prior to the likelihood yields a loss function: Σ (y_n - W·x_n)² + (1/σ₀²) Σ w_i².
The resulting optimization objective is the sum of squares with an L2 regularizer.
An L2 regularizer is the sum of squares of the weights (Euclidean norm).
Using this L2 regularizer can fix the overfitting problem.

Odds represent the ratio of the probability of one outcome to the probability of the other outcome; for example, odds of 50 to 1 mean the probability of one outcome divided by the probability of the other outcome.

Information criteria such as AIC and BIC are approximations to compute the normalizing constant $p(d)$.
There exist many methods to approximate the normalizing constant $p(d)$.
Model selection involves estimating the normalizing constant $p(d)$ for each model and choosing the model with the largest normalizing constant.
Inside a selected model, there is a whole distribution of parameters to be learned.
There are two levels: selecting the model and then learning the parameters within the model.
